Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on admission-control for continuous batching, practical prefetch and KV warmup heuristics that work in VPC/on-prem environments, and an actionable pilot plan. Focused on throughput without regressing tail latency.

Topics:
- Admission control vs. naive max_num_seqs limits
- Prefetch window sizing and eviction policies for KV cache
- Token governor and per-request token limits
- Quantization tradeoffs when optimizing throughput
- VPC/on-prem networking implications for warmup traffic

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Carlos Mendoza: Carlos here, CTO.
[00:07] Priya Iyer: Priya, SRE.
[00:08] Evan Brooks: Evan, ML Eng.
[00:10] Liam O'Connor: Liam from Redwood, SE.
[00:11] Maya Patel: Great. We'll focus on admission control and prefetch playbook, try to be practical. If we run over we'll schedule follow-up.

[00:32] Liam O'Connor: High-level, we want to avoid dropping throughput by over-constraining batching. Admission control sits in the scheduler to gate which reqs enter the continuous batching pipeline. It's more adaptable than a hard max_num_seqs cap because it can bias by tokens and latency budgets.

[01:05] Priya Iyer: Quick clarifying Q: our current staging uses a hard max_num_seqs=4 because we saw tail latency spikes. We're worried raising it might blow up latency.

[01:22] Liam O'Connor: Right, and that's exactly where adaptive admission helps. Instead of just max sequences, you add a token-aware admission score: sequence_length * weight + recent tail latency signal. If score below threshold, admit. That lets short requests bundle more.

[01:48] Carlos Mendoza: So weight for sequence length — do you mean input length, or total tokens including expected output?

[01:55] Liam O'Connor: Mostly a predicted token budget: input_tokens + expected_output_tokens. We use simple historical percentiles per prompt class to estimate expected output. It doesn't have to be ML-perfect.

[02:20] Evan Brooks: Our prompts vary a lot. Some are short instructions, some are multi-turn contexts up to 1k tokens. How do we avoid gaming the estimator?

[02:35] Liam O'Connor: Common approach: classify requests into buckets by prompt template/hash. Keep lightweight stats (P50,P80,P95) of output lengths per bucket. For unknown buckets, fall back to conservative default. Also allow a 'fast lane' header for low-latency critical traffic.

[03:02] Maya Patel: Let's talk prefetched KV warmup — we know KV cache hit rate can massively cut cost and tail. What's your recommended warmup strategy for Stratus?

[03:15] Liam O'Connor: Two-part: proactive prefetch on deploy and reactive prefetch from live traffic. For proactive, run a staged replay of representative prompts against a cold model instance with lower QPS, fetching top-K KV segments to populate caches. For reactive, keep short-lived prefetch windows: when a sequence is admitted but predicted to generate x tokens, prefetch nearby key ranges.

[03:45] Priya Iyer: Proactive replay sounds heavy for on-prem. Network egress and compute are sensitive. Any low-bandwidth options?

[03:55] Liam O'Connor: Yes — you can prefetch at a lower replica concurrency and restrict to the most frequent buckets (e.g., top 10% of prompt hashes). Also use compressed prefetch: prefetch summaries or quantized cache keys rather than full attention maps when supported.

[04:18] Evan Brooks: How do you avoid eviction thrash — e.g., we prefetch too many unique keys and end up evicting useful entries?

[04:26] Liam O'Connor: Key is prefetch budget per model shard. Policies: TTL-based eviction biased by recency + frequency, and a soft prefetch cap measured as fraction of available cache memory. If prefetch would exceed cap, skip lower-ranked buckets. Also track hit-per-prefetch metric to tune window.

[05:00] Carlos Mendoza: Can Redwood tune prefetch windows dynamically? We don't want manual toggles.

[05:07] Liam O'Connor: Yes, the scheduler exposes knobs. We can run an adaptive controller that adjusts the prefetch window size based on observed KV hit rate and tail latency. We usually start conservative then ramp. We'll include a control loop recipe in the playbook.

[05:45] Maya Patel: Let's get a bit specific — propose initial pilot knobs for Stratus staging.

[05:52] Liam O'Connor: Suggested starting point: max_num_seqs soft cap=8, token_limit per request=1024, admission token score threshold tuned to P80_latency target, prefetch window=5 sequences ahead, prefetch_budget=15% of cache memory. Run for 48 hours and measure hit-per-prefetch, tail P99 latency, and cost per 1M tokens.

[06:28] Priya Iyer: The 15% budget — that assumes your cache memory is measurable. On our on-prem it's small. What if it can't hold many entries?

[06:35] Liam O'Connor: Then reduce prefetch_budget to 5-7% and bias prefetch to most frequent buckets only. Also increase reuse threshold so we only prefetch keys with historical hit rate > 0.3.

[07:05] Evan Brooks: We use int8 quantization in some flows. Any interactions with KV caching and quant modes?

[07:14] Liam O'Connor: Yes — quantization affects cache key compatibility if kernel-level representations differ. Use standardized KV serialization across quant modes, or maintain separate cache namespaces per quant profile. Also quant can change per-token compute latency; admission controller should read the model variant latency profile.

[07:45] Carlos Mendoza: Does Redwood keep separate kernels for int8 and int4? We might want int4 for throughput but worried about stability.

[07:54] Liam O'Connor: We support int8 and int4 variants; int4 often gives more throughput but higher variance in quality. For pilot, run int8 in production and int4 in a shadow variant if you want to test tradeoffs without affecting users.

[08:18] Maya Patel: Network implications in VPC/on-prem — particularly for prefetch and warmup traffic — any gotchas?

[08:29] Liam O'Connor: Two big ones: firewall state and cross-AZ bandwidth. Prefetch can add bursts to network if done naively. In VPC we recommend peered subnets with flow-control (e.g., rate-limited prefetch replication) and keep warmup traffic within the same AZ when possible. For on-prem, schedule prefetch during low-business hours and throttle.

[09:00] Priya Iyer: Ok, what about security — storing prefetch indices or prompt traces in the cache might carry PII.

[09:08] Liam O'Connor: Don't store raw prompts as cache keys. Use hashed keys and strip PII before creating prompt buckets. Also ensure cache encryption at rest and KMS for key management. We'll include guidance in the SOC2 checklist we send.

[09:32] Evan Brooks: On the scheduler side, how do you handle mixed workloads — streaming responses vs sync completions — where streaming opens a long-lived connection?

[09:45] Liam O'Connor: Streaming is treated as a separate lane with its own bucket. Admission control counts open streams differently; streams reserve bandwidth by predicted remaining tokens and have higher priority for low-latency. That keeps streaming work from starving batched throughput.

[10:10] Carlos Mendoza: We heard about token governors. Can you describe practical token governor behavior?

[10:17] Liam O'Connor: Token governor enforces per-request and per-customer token consumption rate. For instance, global token_capacity per second, and each request consumes tokens from a leaky bucket. If request would exceed per-request token_limit, it's either truncated or rejected. Also supports soft alerts where requests are deprioritized instead of outright dropped.

[10:45] Maya Patel: Any tips for safe rollout of higher max_num_seqs?

[10:51] Liam O'Connor: Canary: increase for a small subset of traffic (10%), monitor P95/P99 and KV hit rate. Use automatic rollback if tail latency increases more than threshold. Also pair with token governor so single large requests don't fill the batch.

[11:20] Priya Iyer: We want metrics — what should we collect during pilot?

[11:25] Liam O'Connor: Collect: P50/P90/P95/P99 latency, queueing latency in scheduler, batch size distribution, KV hit rate, prefetch hit-per-prefetch, per-request token usage, and throttled/rejected rates. Also CPU/GPU utilization and kernel-level perf counters if available.

[11:55] Evan Brooks: When should we consider turning on interleaved batching vs regular continuous batching?

[12:03] Liam O'Connor: Interleaved batching helps when you have many small requests from different customers — it reduces wasted compute by packing sequences that would otherwise underfill. If your batch size distribution shows a heavy tail of small requests, turn it on for those lanes.

[12:28] Carlos Mendoza: Any memory safety or explosion risks when using interleaving + prefetch?

[12:36] Liam O'Connor: Yes, interleaving with aggressive prefetch can cause memory pressure. Always cap prefetch per-inflight-batch and refuse to prefetch if available GPU memory < threshold. That's in the playbook.

[13:05] Maya Patel: Let's go through a mock playbook run for the next 48 hours — step-by-step.

[13:12] Liam O'Connor: Day 0: baseline metrics collection for 24h with current config. Day 1: enable admission controller with conservative threshold and max_num_seqs soft cap 8 for 10% of traffic. Enable prefetch for top-10 buckets with budget 7%. Day 2: increase traffic slice to 50% if P95 and KV hit improvements are good. Collect snapshots and a final report.

[13:48] Priya Iyer: For the baseline period, what sampling resolution do you need? We can export logs every 30s.

[13:56] Liam O'Connor: 30s is fine for throughput; use 1s resolution for scheduler queueing metrics if possible. Also ingest GPU memory usage at 10s intervals.

[14:20] Evan Brooks: A few quick hypotheses we want to test: 1) prefetch increases effective throughput by >20% for our 80/20 prompt mix; 2) adaptive admission reduces P99 by 15% vs hard max_num_seqs; 3) int4 yields 1.5x throughput but increases P95.

[14:45] Maya Patel: We'll put those in the pilot objective. Any immediate objections or questions?

[14:52] Carlos Mendoza: What about cost accounting — if prefetch increases token read ops, how will that affect billing?

[15:00] Liam O'Connor: Prefetch increases internal token compute but you can measure cost per inference token. We can set a prefetch ROI threshold where prefetch is enabled only if expected hit reduces external token generation cost by more than delta. We'll help you model it.

[15:25] Priya Iyer: Is there a recommended eviction algorithm? LRU variants?

[15:30] Liam O'Connor: We prefer TinyLFU + LRU hybrid for attention caches because it balances recency and frequency. But simpler LRU with a reuse threshold can work if compute for LFU is expensive.

[16:00] Evan Brooks: For on-prem, do you have a smaller runtime artifact that can run without the full control plane during initial warmup?

[16:08] Liam O'Connor: Yes, Redwood provides an offline warmup tool that runs replay and emits a compressed prefetch manifest you can apply locally. That avoids extra control-plane traffic. We'll include it in the playbook.

[16:32] Maya Patel: OK, let's capture concrete knobs we'll adjust during pilot and owners.

[16:40] Liam O'Connor: Knobs: admission_threshold (initial 0.7), soft_max_num_seqs=8, token_limit_per_request=1024, prefetch_window=5, prefetch_budget=15% (staging 7%), prefetch_bucket_rank=top10, reuse_threshold=0.3, eviction_policy=TinyLFU+LRU.

[17:05] Carlos Mendoza: Who owns the rollout?

[17:08] Maya Patel: Redwood will own scheduler/admission config and playbook creation. Stratus will provide representative traffic and spin up staging. So Liam + Priya + Carlos for coordination.

[17:22] Priya Iyer: Network security — we'll need the SOC2 artifacts and network diagram before peering.

[17:27] Maya Patel: We'll send those.

[17:33] Evan Brooks: A few micro details — what metrics indicate prefetch is harmful?

[17:39] Liam O'Connor: Negative hit-per-prefetch (i.e., <0.05), increased eviction churn, or P99 tail increasing beyond 10% of baseline. If any of those happen, reduce prefetch window and budget.

[18:05] Carlos Mendoza: Anything about multi-tenant fairness? We have internal tools and customer-facing endpoints on same cluster.

[18:12] Liam O'Connor: Use per-tenant soft quotas and weighted admission. You can also shard to per-customer pools if exact isolation is required. We recommend soft quotas first, then dedicated pools if noisy neighbors persist.

[18:38] Maya Patel: Let's make sure the playbook includes automated rollback triggers.

[18:44] Liam O'Connor: Agreed — we'll include thresholds for P95/P99/regressions, and an automated rollback via the control plane if thresholds hit.

[19:00] Priya Iyer: Can we get a lightweight demo of the controller UI for the admission thresholds?

[19:05] Maya Patel: We'll schedule a short demo next week.

[19:12] Carlos Mendoza: Anything else on quantization?

[19:17] Liam O'Connor: Keep int8 as the first step. If you shadow int4, monitor semantic regression using small eval set. Don't enable int4 for production until automated quality monitors pass.

[19:33] Evan Brooks: About logging — do we need to log prefetch keys for debugging?

[19:38] Liam O'Connor: Log hashes only and sample. Avoid full prompts. Use rate-limited debug logs to reduce noise.

[19:52] Maya Patel: Okay, I'm going to read back the next steps. Liam will draft the prefetch/eviction playbook and share by Nov 24. Stratus will share prompt set and qps profile by Nov 21. Priya will provision test VPC peering by Nov 22. Redwood to send SOC2 and network diagram. Pilot 48 hours starting once staging is ready.

[20:20] Carlos Mendoza: That sounds good. One last ask — can Redwood include a cost model for prefetch ROI?

[20:27] Liam O'Connor: Yes we have a spreadsheet template, will attach.

[20:31] Maya Patel: Great. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the demo and pilot kickoff.

[20:41] Evan Brooks: Bye.
[20:42] Liam O'Connor: Thanks.
